scenes.visual: Title card 'Why Does a Strawberry Swell?' over a ripe strawberry cartoon. Reuses the first film's COLOUR MAP (both films): maternal chromosome sets = MAGENTA blocks, paternal sets = TEAL blocks; each set is one rounded rectangle block, stacked in a short column beside the cell or tissue it belongs to. Tissue fills: embryo GREEN, endosperm CREAM, seed coat BROWN, fruit wall ORANGE, pollen and tube PALE YELLOW. Plant drawings are flat cartoons labelled 'schematic'. All numbers appear only as on-screen text. Auxin paste is GOLD.

scenes.tts: A strawberry's red flesh is the mother's own tissue, with no chromosomes from the father. So why does it swell only after the flower is pollinated?
scenes.visual: A ripe strawberry cut in half; its red flesh gets a stack of two MAGENTA blocks and an empty TEAL slot. Beside it, an unpollinated flower stays small, label 'not pollinated: no swelling'.
scenes.narration: A strawberry's red flesh is the mother's own tissue, with no chromosomes from the father. So why does it swell only after the flower is pollinated?

scenes.tts: The first film counted the sets in a seed. It ended with the seed coat and fruit wall as the mother's tissue. This film asks what tells her tissue to grow.
scenes.visual: Brief replay of the first film's kernel ledger: GREEN embryo 1 + 1, CREAM endosperm 2 + 1, BROWN/ORANGE coat and fruit wall 2 + 0. It shrinks into a corner and stays as a reference.
scenes.narration: The first film counted the sets in a seed. It ended with the seed coat and fruit wall as the mother's tissue. This film asks what tells her tissue to grow.

scenes.tts: Start with the general rule. After fertilization, the ovule becomes the seed. In most flowering plants, the ovary around it becomes the fruit.
scenes.visual: A generic flower's ovary: the ovule inside turns into a seed with its colour-coded parts, and the ORANGE ovary wall swells into a fruit around it. Labels 'ovule → seed', 'ovary → fruit'.
scenes.narration: Start with the general rule. After fertilization, the ovule becomes the seed. In most flowering plants, the ovary around it becomes the fruit.

scenes.tts: A strawberry flower is unusual. It has many separate ovaries sitting on a dome. The dome is the receptacle, the swollen tip of the flower stalk.
scenes.visual: Strawberry flower in side view (schematic): petals fall away to reveal dozens of tiny ovaries dotted over a dome; the dome is shaded MAGENTA-pink and labelled 'receptacle (tip of the flower stalk)'.
scenes.narration: A strawberry flower is unusual. It has many separate ovaries sitting on a dome. The dome is the receptacle, the swollen tip of the flower stalk.

scenes.tts: After fertilization, each ovary becomes an achene, a small dry fruit holding one seed. Those specks on the surface are the true fruits. The red flesh is swollen receptacle.
scenes.visual: Zoom on one surface speck: it opens in cutaway to show a small seed with GREEN embryo and CREAM endosperm, each with its block stack, inside a thin ORANGE wall, label 'achene: one fruit, one seed'. Zoom out: the dome swells red, label 'flesh = receptacle, 2 + 0'.
scenes.narration: After fertilization, each ovary becomes an achene, a small dry fruit holding one seed. Those specks on the surface are the true fruits. The red flesh is swollen receptacle.

scenes.tts: A fruit whose flesh comes from tissue other than the ovary is called an accessory fruit. Compare a tomato. Its flesh develops from the ovary itself.
scenes.visual: Side by side (schematic): a strawberry labelled 'accessory fruit: flesh from receptacle' and a tomato cut open, its flesh shaded ORANGE and labelled 'flesh from the ovary'. Both fleshes carry a two-MAGENTA stack.
scenes.narration: A fruit whose flesh comes from tissue other than the ovary is called an accessory fruit. Compare a tomato. Its flesh develops from the ovary itself.

scenes.tts: In nineteen fifty, Jean Paul Nitsch asked what makes the receptacle grow. He worked on young receptacles from pollinated flowers, each studded with achenes.
scenes.caption: In 1950, Jean Paul Nitsch asked what makes the receptacle grow. He worked on young receptacles from pollinated flowers, each studded with achenes.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Jean Paul Nitsch, 1950'. Three young green-white receptacles studded with achenes sit side by side on a bench, each tagged 'pollinated'.
scenes.narration: In 1950, Jean Paul Nitsch asked what makes the receptacle grow. He worked on young receptacles from pollinated flowers, each studded with achenes.

scenes.tts: One idea is that the receptacle grows on its own once the flower is pollinated. If so, the achenes should not matter.
scenes.visual: A thought bubble: 'pollinated → receptacle grows, achenes irrelevant?'. A small arrow from 'pollination' points straight to a swelling receptacle, bypassing the achenes.
scenes.narration: One idea is that the receptacle grows on its own once the flower is pollinated. If so, the achenes should not matter.

scenes.tts: So Nitsch removed every achene from some young receptacles. If pollination alone were enough, what would happen to a stripped receptacle?
scenes.visual: Tweezers pick every achene off the middle receptacle, leaving it bare. Question card: 'Stripped receptacle: grow or not?'
scenes.narration: So Nitsch removed every achene from some young receptacles. If pollination alone were enough, what would happen to a stripped receptacle?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer bottom right.

scenes.tts: It did not enlarge. The intact receptacles grew, but the stripped ones stayed small. Growth needed the achenes, not just pollination.
scenes.visual: Time-lapse (schematic): left receptacle with achenes swells red; middle stripped receptacle stays small. The bypass arrow from the earlier thought bubble gets a red cross.
scenes.narration: It did not enlarge. The intact receptacles grew, but the stripped ones stayed small. Growth needed the achenes, not just pollination.

scenes.tts: Next, Nitsch coated some stripped receptacles with a paste containing an auxin, a plant hormone. Those receptacles grew.
scenes.visual: The right receptacle is stripped, then a GOLD paste is brushed on, label 'auxin in paste'. Time-lapse: it swells red like the intact one. Final row: intact 'grew', stripped 'did not', stripped + auxin 'grew'.
scenes.narration: Next, Nitsch coated some stripped receptacles with a paste containing an auxin, a plant hormone. Those receptacles grew.

scenes.tts: Put the three results together. The developing achenes supply a growth signal. Applied auxin can stand in for that signal.
scenes.visual: Arrows from the achenes into the flesh, labelled 'signal'. The GOLD paste appears on the stripped receptacle and sends the same arrows, label 'auxin can mimic it'.
scenes.narration: Put the three results together. The developing achenes supply a growth signal. Applied auxin can stand in for that signal.

scenes.tts: Notice what this does not show. Auxin was enough to restore growth. That does not prove the natural signal is auxin alone. Nor does it show how the signal moves.
scenes.visual: The 'signal' arrows from the achenes stay labelled '?'; a box reads 'auxin: sufficient, not shown to be the only signal'.
scenes.narration: Notice what this does not show. Auxin was enough to restore growth. That does not prove the natural signal is auxin alone. Nor does it show how the signal moves.

scenes.tts: Back to the ledger. The flesh is all mother, two magenta blocks. In a normal fruit, it grows on a signal from the developing achenes.
scenes.visual: The corner ledger returns to centre. The red flesh with its two MAGENTA blocks; arrows labelled 'signal' run into it from the achenes on its surface. A small GOLD paste icon beside them, label 'auxin can stand in'.
scenes.narration: Back to the ledger. The flesh is all mother, two magenta blocks. In a normal fruit, it grows on a signal from the developing achenes.

scenes.tts: This is one experiment, in one kind of accessory fruit. The receptacle is the mother's tissue. But the developing achenes tell it to grow.
scenes.visual: A full strawberry: the achenes glow, the flesh glows MAGENTA, label 'receptacle: mother's tissue', and a bare patch without achenes stays small (schematic, not data), label 'strawberry, Nitsch 1950'.
scenes.narration: This is one experiment, in one kind of accessory fruit. The receptacle is the mother's tissue. But the developing achenes tell it to grow.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. One line: 'The receptacle is the mother's, but the achenes tell it to grow.'
